transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
President Trump has announced that Stephen Miller
will be the next White House Chief of Staff.
Speaking to reporters on his way to Florida just now,
Trump said Susie Wiles, who's currently in the position,
will be moved into another role within the administration.
I think Susie's done a very good job, great job,
but I just wanted to make it.
Stephen's been great, and we've got to make moves.
NPR's Danielle Kurt-Slaben reports the move signals
the administration is not backing down after blistering
Republican losses in this year's midterms.
President Trump announced the personnel change on social
media, saying Miller will take over the position on
Monday, November 9th.
Wiles worked with the Trump 2020 campaign in Florida
and has served as Chief of Staff in this White House
from day one of this administration.
She's the first woman to hold the position.
In his social media post, Trump says she will be moving
to the Trump political operation.
Miller has been a fixture in Trump's circle since 2016
and is considered one of the president's most trusted
and aggressive advisers.
He is known in particular for being an architect
of the president's anti-immigration policies.
Danielle Kurt-Slaben, NPR News, the White House.
Democratic Senator Tim Kaine says Congress should use
its spending power to rein in President Trump's
military operations against Iran.
If you won't follow the Constitution, the statute,
or the concurrent resolution, our only choice is to
use the appropriations process to forbid funding for
war operations unless the president gets the legally
required authorization by Congress.
The House and Senate voted in June to direct Trump
to withdraw U.S. forces from the conflict.
The Virginia Democrat says the president has
disregarded that vote.
The White House argues that Trump has the
constitutional authority to defend U.S. forces
against Iranian attacks.
Google, meta and TikTok are challenging a new
California law designed to protect children from
potentially addictive social media features.
NPR's Katie McHugh reports the law is set to take
effect in January.
California's new law prohibits social media
platforms from offering features considered
exploitative to users younger than 18.
That includes using algorithms to keep kids
scrolling and auto-playing video.
The law also requires social media companies to
delete children's accounts with those features.
Yet the companies argue that the law is
unconstitutional and violates the First Amendment.
The lawsuits come amid growing scrutiny of tech
companies' impact on children.
Meta, Google, TikTok and Snap are facing thousands
of lawsuits from families, school districts and
state governments who allege their platforms
contribute to a youth mental health crisis.
Katie McHugh, NPR News, New York.
On Wall Street, the Dow was down 96 points.
This is NPR News.
Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy is making what
his office calls "remarkable progress" in his
recovery from a stroke.
The Democrat was hospitalized last week after
his arm went numb.
Murphy says he will not return to the Senate on
Monday and will spend the next several weeks
recovering at a rehabilitation center.
A new round of bomb threats has forced emergency
landings in Europe for the third day this week
with fighter jets escorting planes.
Several news outlets have also been targeted.
The Irish government says it doesn't know who's
behind the threats but believes they're likely
part of a coordinated effort to cause disruption.
Esme Nicholson reports from Berlin.
On Wall Street, the Dow was down 95 points.
The NASDAQ up 300 points.
